title: Vermont Republic
capsule: The Vermont Republic declared independence on 15 January 1777, when delegates from 28 New England towns rejected overlapping jurisdictional claims of New York, New Hampshire, and British Quebec, initially calling themselves the Republic of New Connecticut before adopting the name Vermont on 2 June 1777. Under long-serving Governor Thomas Chittenden, the republic minted its own copper coinage, operated a postal service, and conducted diplomacy with the Continental Congress and European powers; its 1777 constitution, modeled on Pennsylvania's, was among the first in the Americas to prohibit adult slavery. After New York finally consented to Vermont statehood in 1790 and Vermont paid $30,000 to settle land disputes, a convention voted 105–2 for union and Vermont entered the United States on 4 March 1791 as the fourteenth state.
attestation: Boundaries from Seshat Cliopatria (Bennett et al., Scientific Data 2025; CC BY 4.0), digitized from standard historical atlases at ~0.07° resolution. Vermont's claimed territory — essentially the present state's boundaries — is well documented from the 1777 declaration; the disputed boundary with New York was not definitively settled until 1790, introducing some ambiguity in the northeastern extent.
